strengths: Timely and well-motivated theoretical formalization of collaborative multi-agent reasoning, bridging the Transformer expressivity literature with classical parallel computing and communication complexity.
Clear delineation into three fundamental regimes of depth-communication tradeoffs across distinct algorithmic classes (associative recall, state tracking via monoids, and k-hop reasoning).
Mathematically rigorous proofs for both upper and lower bounds within the Unique Hard Attention Transformer (UHAT) framework.
Comprehensive synthetic experiments using open-weights LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, EXAONE-32B) that faithfully validate the theoretical depth vs. communication scaling tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The theoretical framework relies on the Unique Hard Attention Transformer (UHAT) abstraction with potentially growing width d, which abstracts away finite-precision and soft-attention dynamics present in real-world models.

Evaluation is restricted strictly to controlled synthetic problems (parity, S5 tracking, synthetic relation chains); validating whether these scaling tradeoffs hold on standard real-world multi-agent QA or reasoning benchmarks would significantly increase practical impact.

Minor presentation and drafting issues: missing repository URL in the Reproducibility Statement on page 10, minor typographical errors in Definition 3.1 item 4 ('outgoing edges edge with the same label') and Appendix C.2 ('outpts this agent's ID'), and mismatched references (e.g., referencing Table 2 on page 5 when only Table 1 exists).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: while multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly popular empirically, their formal expressive capacity and fundamental communication-depth tradeoffs have remained largely uncharacterized.

Proposes a clean, rigorous theoretical formalization of multi-agent reasoning systems grounded in Transformer expressivity (UHAT), establishing clear definitions of computation depth (wall-clock time), graph size (total computation), and communication budget.

Identifies and characterizes three distinct regimes of multi-agent reasoning through representative algorithmic families (associative recall, state tracking, and k-hop reasoning), providing tight upper and lower bounds that illuminate when communication enables parallel speedups versus when it represents an unavoidable bottleneck.

The theoretical insights directly inform practical multi-agent protocol design, notably highlighting the bottleneck of single-manager aggregation (e.g., Chain-of-Agents) and showing how tree-structured prefix-sum cascades can achieve logarithmic depth.

Complements theoretical derivations with controlled empirical evaluations across multiple open-source models (Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, EXAONE-3.5-32B), closely corroborating the predicted tradeoffs between communication, depth, and accuracy.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is conducted strictly on synthetic algorithmic tasks (bitstring parity, synthetic key-value recall, synthetic entity-relation chains). While understandable for tightly validating asymptotic theory, demonstrations on realistic NLP/reasoning benchmarks (e.g., multi-hop QA or long-document reasoning) would strengthen practical impact.

The theoretical analysis assumes Unique Hard Attention Transformers (UHAT) with potentially growing embedding dimension for positional encodings, which—while standard in recent expressivity literature—does not capture all nuances of fixed-dimension soft-attention Transformers operating in practice.

In the empirical section, real LLMs occasionally exhibit instruction-following drift (e.g., repeating queries or formatting verbosely), which adds constant/linear token overhead and causes slight discrepancies with theoretical depth curves in high-communication settings.

strengths: Timely and relevant motivation: While multi-agent LLM frameworks (such as MapReduce, Chain-of-Agents, debate) are proliferated in practice, theoretical foundations regarding their expressivity, communication requirements, and parallel speedups have been largely absent.

Clear conceptual taxonomy: Categorizing multi-agent reasoning tasks into three distinct regimes—embarrassingly parallel with constant overhead (associative recall), depth-communication tradeoffs via parallel scan/prefix sums (state tracking), and inherently sequential communication bottlenecks (k-hop reasoning)—provides an intuitive and structured framework.

Rigorous grounding in Transformer expressivity: Formulating multi-agent computation as a DAG of unique hard attention Transformer (UHAT) state nodes and communication edges connects multi-agent reasoning to established formal language / circuit complexity literature on Transformers.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The underlying algorithmic ideas for the three regimes—broadcast/filtering, parallel prefix sum (recursive parallel scan), and iterative pointer chasing / query expansion—are classical parallel and distributed computing primitives (reminiscent of standard PRAM/work-depth analysis). Embedding these into the UHAT formalism is a neat exercise, but the resulting depth and communication bounds offer few conceptual surprises beyond classical parallel complexity.

Gap between formal model and realistic LLM behavior: The theory relies on idealized UHAT Transformers with hard attention, exact positional encodings, and single-token communication primitives. Real-world LLM multi-agent systems rely on softmax attention over natural language messages, where instruction-following errors, noise accumulation, and context degradation frequently dominate performance (as observed even in the authors' synthetic experiments in Figure 4b).

Evaluation restricted to synthetic toy tasks: The empirical validation is conducted entirely on synthetic benchmarks (bit parity, S5 permutations, key-value lookup, synthetic relationship graph hops). While synthetic setups help isolate parameters, there is no evaluation on standard NLP reasoning or multi-agent benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA, long-form summarization, GSM8K multi-agent setups) to demonstrate practical applicability or predictive power on real workloads.

Hand-waving and simplicity in lower bound proofs: Some lower bounds (e.g., Proposition 4.7 depth lower bound) simply restate the definition Size / w <= Depth without deeper information-theoretic or communication-complexity analysis specific to the neural architecture. Similarly, the proof of Proposition C.2 in the appendix is quite informal regarding how layers and positional encodings scale uniformly across input lengths.

strengths: Pioneering and timely theoretical formalization: The paper provides one of the first rigorous frameworks to analyze the expressivity, computation depth, size, and communication complexity of LLM-based multi-agent reasoning systems.

Clear categorization into three distinct operational regimes: The paper establishes rigorous matching or near-matching upper and lower bounds for three core algorithmic families—associative recall (constant depth and communication), state tracking (logarithmic/fractional depth reduction at linear communication cost), and k-hop reasoning (inherently sequential depth and communication scaling with hop count).

Principled architectural implications: The theoretical results offer valuable guidance for system designers, specifically highlighting when flat worker-manager topologies (e.g., Chain-of-Agents) create aggregation bottlenecks and provably benefit from hierarchical prefix-sum cascades or sequential multi-hop handoffs.

Comprehensive theoretical development: The paper includes thorough proofs for the main propositions, an analysis of error propagation in hierarchical trees (Appendix D), and an interesting super-polynomial separation between majority voting / self-consistency and communicative multi-agent protocols (Appendix H).

Clean empirical validation: Experiments across multiple open-weight models (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, EXAONE) align closely with the predicted theoretical tradeoffs between computation depth, communication volume, and task difficulty.
weaknesses: Idealized model of Transformers: The theoretical analysis is based on unique hard attention Transformers (UHAT). While the authors discuss the connection to fixed-precision soft-attention Transformers in Appendix I, UHAT remains an idealized abstraction that does not capture continuous soft attention dynamics, continuous value accumulation, or training dynamics.

Evaluation restricted to synthetic algorithmic benchmarks: While synthetic tasks (needle-in-a-haystack, bitstring parity, S5 permutations, synthetic relational chains) are appropriate for validating foundational algorithmic properties, the paper lacks evaluation on naturalistic, complex multi-agent tasks (e.g., real-world multi-document QA, code repositories, or complex agentic tool-use environments).

Rigid input partitioning assumption: The framework largely assumes inputs are partitioned disjointly across worker agents, which models map-reduce / chunking paradigms well but does not directly capture settings where agents share overlapping context, operate asynchronously, or maintain shared dynamic memory stores.

strengths: Principled and timely formalization: The paper introduces a rigorous theoretical framework modeling multi-agent LLM reasoning as labeled directed acyclic graphs grounded in Transformer expressivity (specifically unique hard-attention Transformers, UHAT). This bridges the gap between Transformer expressivity theory and the rapidly growing empirical literature on multi-agent architectures.

Comprehensive characterization of trade-offs: The work identifies and proves tight upper and lower bounds for three distinct communication and depth regimes across fundamental algorithmic families: associative recall (constant depth and communication), state tracking (depth speedup via parallel scan / prefix-sum at the expense of linear communication), and k-hop reasoning (strictly sequential depth O(k) across partitioned facts).

Conceptual depth and separation results: The authors provide compelling theoretical separations, such as showing in Appendix H that a tree-structured protocol (PrefixSum) achieves exponential advantage over naive majority voting / self-consistency strategies for state tracking under logarithmic depth constraints.

Extensive theoretical and empirical analysis: The submission includes 41 pages of comprehensive proofs, error modeling under noisy LLM nodes (Lemma D.1), extensions to soft-attention fixed-precision Transformers (Appendix I), and empirical validation across multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, EXAONE) demonstrating that observed token usage and wall-clock proxies match the predicted theoretical frontiers.
weaknesses: Reliance on synthetic tasks: While algorithmic benchmarks (parity, S5 permutation tracking, synthetic relation composition) are standard for validating expressivity theory, the empirical evaluation lacks testing on real-world long-context multi-agent benchmarks (e.g., complex multi-hop QA or agentic coding/planning pipelines).

Restricted communication model: The framework primarily models disjoint input partitioning and message passing via appended tokens. While well-aligned with map-reduce and chunk-processing paradigms (e.g., Chain-of-Agents, LLM-MapReduce), it does not directly capture interactive paradigms with full context sharing or unstructured multi-agent debate.

Incremental proof techniques: Several lower bound results rely on direct reductions to established results in circuit complexity and communication complexity (e.g., Amiri et al., 2025; Tesson & Thérien, 2002; Aspnes et al., 1991). The novelty stems primarily from synthesizing these results into a unified multi-agent LLM abstraction rather than developing novel mathematical machinery.

Practical execution noise in empirical verification: As acknowledged in Section 5.2, real pretrained LLMs suffer from prompt verbosity, instruction drift, and formatting overhead, causing minor deviations from idealized theoretical scaling curves (e.g., in Figure 4(b) at higher communication budgets).

strengths: Principled and timely formalization: The paper proposes a rigorous graph-theoretic framework for analyzing multi-agent reasoning systems that naturally extends the Transformer expressivity literature (causally masked unique hard attention Transformers, UHAT) to distributed multi-agent setups.

Clear taxonomy of complexity regimes: The authors successfully identify and formally prove the existence and optimality of three distinct operational regimes (recall with O(1) communication and depth, state tracking with a depth-communication tradeoff via parallel scan/prefix sum, and multi-hop reasoning where depth cannot be accelerated beyond hop count in the worst case).

Tight theoretical results: The paper derives matching upper and lower bounds on computation depth, communication budget, and overall size across all three task families, accompanied by thorough and technically sound proofs in the appendix (including connections to fixed-precision softmax Transformers and separations against majority voting).

Convincing empirical alignment: Controlled experiments using modern LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, EXAONE-3.5) on synthetic benchmarks (Needle-in-a-haystack, Parity/S5 permutations, and k-hop relations) validate the theoretical tradeoffs between communication volume, depth/token usage, and task accuracy.

Insightful contextualization: Section 6 and Appendix B provide valuable conceptual comparisons to classical parallel computing paradigms (e.g., PRAM, MPC, BSP) and clearly elucidate why the inductive bias and expressivity of the underlying Transformer processor distinguish this theory from standard parallel computing frameworks.
weaknesses: Focus on synthetic benchmarks: The empirical evaluation is primarily conducted on stylized synthetic tasks (Parity, permutation tracking, synthetic relation chains). While appropriate for validating theoretical asymptotic behaviors, demonstrating these tradeoffs on realistic long-context multi-agent workflows (e.g., multi-document QA, code repository analysis) would further strengthen practical relevance.

Hard-coded communication topology: The theoretical protocols and empirical implementations rely on fixed, predetermined communication topologies (such as static prefix-sum trees or fixed worker-coordinator pipelines). In real-world multi-agent systems, agents often dynamically decide when and with whom to communicate.

Reliance on prior lower bounds: Key technical lower bounds borrow heavily from known results in circuit complexity and Transformer expressivity (e.g., Amiri et al., 2025 for Parity lower bounds; Tesson & Thérien, 2002 for permutation communication complexity), though adapting them cleanly to the multi-agent DAG framework remains a valuable contribution.

Minor presentation artifacts: Appendix I contains phrasing suggesting a response to past reviewers ('A reviewer asks about the implications of our results...'), and Definition 3.1 (item 4) has a minor typo ('(ii) outgoing edges edge with the same label').
